assignment: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.
essay_1:
Why You Should Ask More Than One Person

Last spring I had to pick an elective for high school, and I asked my older cousin first. He told me to take computer science because "that's where the jobs are." I almost signed up right away. Then I decided to ask my art teacher, my best friend, and my mom too. They all gave me different advice, and in the end I understood my own choice way better than I would have after just one talk. That taught me a good lesson. Asking more than one person for advice usually helps you make a better and smarter decision. Getting a few opinions helps you see things you missed, balances out people's bias, and gives you a fuller and clearer picture of your choice.

The first reason to ask several people is that each person only sees part of a situation. Nobody has lived every life, so their advice comes from their own experience. My cousin loves computer science because he is great at math and he enjoys puzzles. His advice was honest and kind, and it fit him well. It just did not fit me as well. When I talked to my art teacher, she smiled and pointed out that I spend most of my free time drawing. She said the digital design class mixes art with technology, which sounded exciting to me. I had never even thought about that class. One person showed me one door, and the second person showed me a door I did not know was there. When you collect advice from different people, all the little pieces fit together into something closer to the whole truth.

The second reason is that everyone has some bias, even when they care about you and want to help. Parents may want their kids to pick the safe choice because they love them and worry about them getting hurt. Friends may want you to pick whatever keeps you close to them, since they enjoy your company and hate being left out. A salesperson wants you to buy the thing they are selling. These people are not lying. Their wishes can still quietly shape what they say. Think about someone buying a used car. If they only ask the dealer, they will hear that the car is in great shape and a good deal. If they also ask a friend who is a mechanic and read reviews from other owners, they might find out that the car has a bad transmission problem that costs a lot to fix. By hearing from people who want different things, the buyer gets a fair and honest view and can avoid a costly mistake.

Third, hearing different opinions makes you think harder about what you value. When two people you trust disagree, you have to ask yourself which reason makes more sense and what matters most to you. My mom told me to pick the class with the easiest grading to keep my GPA safe and strong. My friend told me to pick whatever sounded the most fun. I realized I had to decide for myself if I cared more about good grades or about enjoying the class. Thinking about that was hard and confusing at first, and I was worried I would pick wrong. Answering it made me feel proud and confident about my final choice. A single piece of advice can make a choice feel easy, and it can also let you skip the real thinking that a good decision needs.

Asking more than one person also protects you from simple mistakes. Doctors know this well, which is why patients who need a serious surgery are often told to get a second opinion. A second doctor might read the same test results in a new way, suggest a safer treatment, or agree that the first doctor was right. Either way, the patient wins. If the doctors agree, the patient can move forward with more trust and hope. If they disagree, the patient has caught a dangerous error in time. The same idea works for smaller things too, like asking two teachers to read your essay before you turn it in. One teacher might catch a confusing sentence that the other teacher missed, and your essay gets better.

Of course, asking too many people can get stressful and overwhelming, and in the end the choice still belongs to you. Advice is a helpful tool, and you still have to use your own judgment. The goal is not to count votes and go with the most popular answer. The goal is to collect enough good ideas to make a smart choice. It works best to ask people who know different things, like an expert, someone who has been through the same thing, and someone who knows you well and wants the best for you. That works a lot better than asking ten people who all think the same way and share the same blind spots.

In the end, I picked the digital design class, and it became my favorite class of the whole year. Not every project was easy, and some days I struggled, but I liked the work and I made good friends. I would never have found that class if I had only listened to my first piece of advice, and I might have been stuck in a class I did not enjoy. Talking to several people helped me see more options, notice hidden bias, and understand what I truly wanted. Whether you are picking a class, a car, or a medical treatment, listening to more than one voice gives you the best chance to choose well.
essay_2:
Why You Should Ask More Than One Person

Last spring I had to pick an elective for high school. First I asked my older cousin and he said take computer science because "thats where the jobs are." I almost signed up right then. But I didnt. I also asked my art teacher, my best friend, and my mom. They all said something different, and by the end I understood my choice way better than if I only talked to one person. So I think asking more than one person for advice usually helps you make a better choice. It helps because other people see stuff you miss, it balances out peoples bias, and it makes you think about what you really want.

The first reason is that every person only sees part of the situation. Nobody has done everything, so their advice comes from there own life. My cousin loves computer science because hes good at math and he likes puzzles. His advice was honest but it fit him, not really me. Then I talked to my art teacher. She said I spend pretty much all my free time drawing, and theres a digital design class that mixes art and technology. I never even thought about that class. My cousin showed me one door and my teacher showed me a door I didnt know was there. When you ask a bunch of people, all there little pieces kind of fit together and you get closer to the real answer.

The second reason is that everybody has some bias, even if they mean well. Parents want you to pick the safe thing because they worry about you. Your friends might want you to pick whatever keeps you with them. A salesperson just wants you to buy what there selling. They are not lying exactly, but what they want can change what they tell you. For example say someone is buying a used car. If they only ask the dealer, the dealer is going to say the car is great and its a good deal. But if they ask a friend who is a mechanic to look under the hood, and they read reviews from people who own that car, they might find out that car has transmission problems a lot. When you hear from people who want different things, you can tell when one person is leaning to far one way.

Third, when people tell you different things it makes you think harder about what you actually care about. If two people you trust disagree, you cant just do what they say. You have to figure out whose reasons make more sense and what matters to you. My mom told me to take the class with the easiest grading so my GPA stays good. My friend told me to take whatever sounded the most fun. So I had to decide if I cared more about grades or fun. That was kind of uncomfortable to think about, but after I figured it out I felt alot more sure. If you only get one piece of advice the decision feels easy, but you might skip the thinking you really need to do.

Asking more than one person also stops you from making dumb mistakes. Doctors know this, thats why people who need a big surgery get told to get a second opinion. The second doctor might look at the same tests and see something different, or have a treatment thats less risky, or they might just agree with the first doctor. Either way the patient wins. If both doctors agree, the patient can feel better about going ahead. If they dont agree, the patient found out about a big problem before it was to late. This works for small stuff too, like having two teachers read your essay before you turn it in. One of them might catch a confusing sentence the other one missed.

Now, asking to many people can get overwhelming, and at the end of the day its still your decision. Advice is like a tool, it doesnt replace your own thinking. The point isnt to count votes and go with whatever most people said. The point is to get enough different views so you know what your doing. Its better to ask people who know different things, like an expert, someone who went through the same thing, and someone who knows you really well, then to ask ten people who are all the same.

In the end I picked the digital design class and it was my favorite class all year. I never would of found it if I just listened to my cousin. Talking to a few different people helped me see more choices, notice when people were biased, and figure out what I really wanted. Whether your picking a class, a car, or what to do about a medical problem, listening to more than one person gives you the best chance to choose right.
